questions.title: Game: met the cell, simple and real
Why an electron microscope?
opts: They are much too small: you need an electron microscope to see them.
They have no colour, so no stain can ever make them visible to you.
They move too fast in the cytosol, so the picture is always blurred.
They are hidden inside the nucleus, behind its two membranes.

questions.title: Game: glucose, oxygen and amino acids entered; carbon dioxide left
The red blood cell
opts: It is a whole cell: far too large to pass through the membrane.
It carries no oxygen, so the cell membrane does not let it pass.
It is a waste product, so the cell membrane never lets it enter.
It has no nucleus, so no carrier protein can carry it inside.

questions.title: Game: released energy by aerobic respiration
Energy in the cell
opts: Respiration releases energy from glucose, and the cell uses it for its work.
Mitochondria make new energy from nothing, then store it inside glucose.
Glucose is made from energy in the mitochondria during aerobic respiration.
The nucleus uses all of the energy, so it needs the most mitochondria.

questions.title: The folded membrane
opts: The folds give a large surface, where most of the energy is released.
The folds make the mitochondrion stronger, so it does not burst.
The folds store glucose, ready for respiration later in the day.
The folds help the mitochondrion to move quickly through the cytosol.

questions.title: Game: found the gene and copied it; the copy left the nucleus
A copy, not the gene
opts: The DNA stays in the nucleus: only copies leave, through its pores.
The DNA is too small to carry the instructions as far as a ribosome.
The copy is made of protein, so a ribosome can use it immediately.
The gene is made in the cytoplasm, so it can never enter the nucleus.

questions.title: What chromosomes look like
opts: Long, thin threads spread through the nucleus
Short X shapes in a line in the middle of the cell
Small round balls, one inside each nuclear pore
Flat sheets folded neatly round the nucleolus

questions.title: Game: built the two ribosome parts
What the nucleolus makes
opts: The two parts of ribosomes, from RNA and proteins
The copy of the amylase gene, from amino acids
The membrane of the nucleus, from lipids and sugar
The energy for the nucleus, from glucose and oxygen

questions.title: Game: joined the amino acids; chose the rough ER
The signal
opts: It takes the ribosome to the rough ER, where proteins that leave the cell are made.
It makes the nucleus produce a second copy of the amylase gene for the cell.
It joins the two parts of the ribosome together after they leave the nucleus.
It gives the ribosome the energy it needs to join the amino acids together.

questions.title: How long?
opts: About 90 seconds
About 9 seconds
About 900 seconds
About 5 seconds

questions.title: Game: made the chain inside the rough ER; folded it
So much rough ER
opts: It makes a lot of protein, which it releases from the cell.
It stores a lot of glucose in its rough ER, for respiration.
It releases most of its energy by respiration in its rough ER.
It keeps extra copies of all its DNA inside the rough ER.

questions.title: The right shape
opts: Starch must fit into its active site, or amylase cannot digest it.
The right shape makes amylase light enough to float in saliva.
Only the right shape can pass through a pore in the nucleus.
A folded chain needs less energy than a straight chain to move.

questions.title: Game: made lipids for the ER membrane
Rough or smooth?
opts: Rough ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER has none and makes lipids.
Rough ER makes lipids for membranes; smooth ER has ribosomes and makes proteins.
Rough ER is found inside the nucleus; smooth ER is in the cytoplasm around it.
Rough ER releases the energy of the cell; smooth ER stores it as glucose.

questions.title: Game: sorted and packaged the proteins
Why sort?
opts: Each protein works in one place, so it must be sent to the right one.
Only sorted proteins can be digested by the enzymes in your saliva.
Sorting gives each protein the energy it needs to fold into its shape.
A protein that is not sorted becomes a lipid inside the Golgi.

questions.title: Game: steered the vesicle to the top of the cell
Why energy?
opts: Each step it takes along the microtubule uses energy.
It must make a new microtubule before it can walk.
It digests the vesicle, so that the amylase is released.
It must split every glucose molecule in two first.

questions.title: Game: exocytosis after the nerve message
The signal to release
opts: A message from a nerve, when you smell or taste food
The vesicles become full, so they open by themselves
Glucose that enters the cell from the blood after a meal
Starch that enters the cell through the cell membrane

questions.title: Where the membrane goes
opts: It becomes part of the cell membrane.
It is digested by the amylase inside it.
It leaves the cell in the saliva, as a bubble.
It becomes a new ribosome in the cell.

questions.title: Game: tested the amylase on starch
The control
opts: It is a control: it shows what happens to the starch without saliva.
It makes the iodine solution darker, so the colours are clearer.
It gives the amylase more water, so it digests starch faster.
It cools the spotting tile, so the amylase does not get too hot.

questions.title: Reading the result
opts: There was no starch left: the amylase had digested it into sugar.
More starch was made from the sugar that the saliva contains.
The amylase had changed the orange-brown iodine into starch.
The water in saliva diluted the starch until no colour could form.
